Maybe it was just me but this reminded me of Saturdays of yore. It reinforced several things I keep telling new solvers: take some breaks, jump around, don’t give up, and don’t hold one to every answer you think you are sure of.

For example, BITTER and SEDERPLATE should have been slam dunks for me; but I was too bamboozled by dish as a type of food and LIE before ISM (lies are certainly meant to be believed); then I misread 45 across and had FILLEDAGAP. It wasn’t until I said it’s got to be BITTER, and dropped my assumptions, that I finally got that corner. I was never going to get HAIRMETAL and GRACEPALEY on my own, and tried to intuit the poison classification as ending with LIC, which gave me the very sensible idea that the queue clue ended with LINE. So sometimes you just gotta start over.

Other things I held on to for far too long were HENS before EWES, CAST party before HOST, RECORDBOOK before RECIPE (which seemed like a lousy place to keep secrets), BOAT___ before BEER___, NIGHTSHIRT before DRESS, AQUA and TEAL before CYAN, so every corner was pulling teeth to me. Riffing on 47D [Material theorized as a possible cause of ancient Rome's decline, given its widespread use]...

It's not out of the question that lead (Pb) is responsible for the current decline of the Western world.  We know this happens with leaded paint, but I think it's much worse than that.

Consider: tetraethyl lead was a fuel additive for the early decades of automobiles, right up until it was finally phased out in the 70s and 80s.  Burning it doesn't destroy the lead--it spreads it into the environment.  And it's still there.

So, for most of baby boomers' lives the air was literally strewn with lead from car exhaust. 

Lead is a lifetime poison--once it's in the body, it doesn't leave.  It accumulates.  The Pb blood level may decrease a bit when one is not actively being poisoned, but Pb trapped in bones will continue to leach into the blood stream.

What we are seeing in the world today might be, at least in part, due to widespread mental degradation due to the leaded gasolines.  We could very easily be getting stupider, but at a slow rate we don't really notice it.

Or, this could be totally wrong.

The point I'm making is that we just don't know.  Humans can and have found ways to poison themselves with their technology (arsenic in cosmetics, radium in watch-making, etc).  And 1) we are, for a period, incapable of determining it's happening, and 2) we can't easily ameliorate the problem, because doing so hurts profits.

Then again, I'm just a tree hugger.

The downs in the NE were Monday-level so that part of the puzzle felt like one huge gimme. The NW was very doable, too.

But then there was the rest of the puzzle. I had almost nothing in the middle, SW and SE sections (LEAD and ETON were my only gimmes there). I started at the mostly empty grid for 20 minutes and I made some desperate guesses, but they all turned out to be wrong in the end. FISHsAucE crossed well with CITE, as did "wealthy" with "aqua". Without Google there was no way out of the mess I created.

As is often the case, I simply didn't know the names and things that featured there. I've never heard of CASH APP, CUREL, Elizabeth Bishop and her "One ART", Discover, "The Duck Variations", JERSEY CITY, and GRACE PALEY - I ended up having to look up all that to finish. For SEDER PLATE I relied on crosses, only - I've learned of SEDER from these puzzles, but I expected a dish to have a less ... generic (?) name. Not knowing what that was, I didn't get BITTER without loads of crosses, either.

As crosses revealed the entry, I found TRUE LEAVES very weird, too. It's not a term I've seen before and I can't recall its Polish equivalent.

[Plant parts that develop as a seedling grows]

The first leaves of a plant seedling are called cotyledons, and the true leaves come a little later, once the seedling has developed roots or some vitality, that's when the true leaves come in. What I love about the clue is that it can be used for both kinds of leaves.

At least as far as xword info knows, cotyledons has never appeared here as clue or fill.

I have been waiting a long time for cotyledons to appear in a puzzle here, so when I saw that clue, my heart started beating with joy. At last, cotyledons will have their day in the sun! 

But no. "True leaves." Don't they know cotyledons are the more deserving of that name? True leaves are mere pretenders to the throne!  How much longer must I endure this curel torture?

Second time this week I've been emued.  I actually did math for this post and I don't want it to go to waste, so here's the executive summary.

This puzzle was a paradigm of freshness.  More than three-quarters (.76) of the grid’s white squares belong to answers that have appeared either never- or once-before!  Three quarters!  And the answer set is clean!  And the answers are interesting!

My outing was filled with giddy gets, and the cluing had wordplay and deft misdirection that gave my brain the work it loves.

I felt like I earned this one, and that’s the hallmark of a proper Saturday.

I kind of enjoyed this puzzle.  Passover is a mainstream enough Jewish holiday for an Asian like me to figure out the solutions.  But I struggled with the Japanese skincare brand.  CUREL is not as mainstream SK-II or Biore.  Curel as a Japanese skincare brand is as obscure as Shmini Atzerat as a Jewish holiday.  Maybe it’s just me.  I’ve fairly oily skin, and therefore didn’t know that Curel is the go to for intensive moisturising.

So …  I am an expert solver who virtually always solves even the hardest Saturdays with no lookups. I don’t often call foul but in this instance I have to do so on CUREL/TRUELEAVES. 

(I am actually not that worked up about this; I don’t pay attention to streaks, and I do this for fun — and this puzzle was still fun. But I think it’s also worth a mention …)

CUREL is undeducible: if you don’t know the brand itself, CeREL is perfectly reasonable. 

TRUE LEAVES, while an actual term (i.e., not green paint), as I learned from Google, is still a fairly specialized one. To someone who has never heard the phrase, which I imagine is most people who are neither gardeners nor biologists, TReE LEAVES seems equally apt. 

This is a place where IMO the editors should have stepped in. Instead of the very general [Plant parts that develop as a seedling grows], a fairer clue might have been [Gardening term for plant parts that develop as a seedling grows], which would have indicated a specialized term. 

An even better clue would have been [Plant parts that develop after cotyledons]. Now, I had no idea before today what a “cotyledon” is (it is a seed leaf that precedes the true leaf). But the clue would have signaled that something was up, and I would have been more careful. 

With either clue I would have at least paused on TReE LEAVES — not sure I would have gotten it but might have led me to question CeREL or run the alphabet on that square. As it was I was completely mystified.

I, too, spent a solid 5 minutes flyspecking and second-guessing CeREL before it occurred to me that TRUELEAVES might be a thing…at which time CUREL suddenly rang a bell. Utterly brutal crossing. Keep it coming!

Apart from that, this was a pretty standard post-Easening Saturday in terms of difficulty, but I absolutely loved some of the clueing. In particular: HAIRMETAL, RECIPEBOOK, CALC, BOLO, CRANES.

I thought I'd solved this with one cheat.  I cheated on ALISON by typing in "actress BRIE" when I had NBRIE in my grid.  It always seems less cheatsy to use what I've already figured out than to type in the info that the clue provides, like Trudy and Mad Men.

 But I still had to get past TEAL for the turquoise relative.  Initially needing to choose between TEAL and AQUA, TEAL was "confirmed" by the A and I never questioned it.  Who in the world would think of CYAN?  Isn't that an entirely different shade of blue?

So TEAL screwed up that section of the puzzle.  Only when MONEYED finally came in -- you try to make a word meaning "rich" out of MOL???? -- did I finally get CYAN.  Whew!!!!  Finished!!!!

But no such luck.  Rex reveals that TREE LEAVES/CEREL is wrong.  Which I never in a million years would have known if I hadn't glanced at his writeup.  And therefore, after all that hard work, I ended up with a DNF anyway.

One of the great blessings of solving on paper is that you don't always know if you have a DNF.  I imagine I would have been happier today not knowing.

What an incredible amount of work this was.  I respect this puzzle like crazy, but I don't necessarily love it.  It's not a very nice day out and maybe I'll go back to bed:)

A huge recurring misunderstanding about crossword puzzles is that puzzles are meant to hinge upon *knowing* the trivia. But they’re not! The idea is to force most solvers (the majority who are presumed not to know the less-obvious trivia entries right off the bat) to fill in enough crosses to make good inferences.

For instance, in today’s puzzle, I very much doubt any solver immediately got “Seder plate” without any crosses; but the average solver *is* expected to be able to recognize/infer that once a few crosses are in place. And while *some* solvers surely got “Jersey City” with minimal help from crosses, the answer basically fills itself in once you have the leading “JE” and enough of the bottom crossers to infer “CITY”.
